prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map places the ground at the bottom and the large curved post in the near foreground, roughly 0.3–0.8 m from the camera, while the stone structure is about 1–2 m ahead and the dark vegetation and water lie several metres farther away. Across the five frames, the post shifts from the right edge toward the centre and then back right, indicating that the wearer turns or moves around it; the stone structure remains ahead-left to centre and changes little in distance. The wearer’s partly visible hands are within arm’s reach, and the cat in frames 4–5 appears roughly 1–2 m ahead-right, separated from the stone structure by about 1 m laterally. The map makes foreground-versus-background separation and the post’s occlusion of the scene clearer than RGB, but its smooth gradients, weak object boundaries, and inconsistent treatment of the cat, water, and thin vegetation make metric distances approximate.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map consistently isolates the central stone-covered structure, but labels it “umbrella,” so its mask is useful for location and extent rather than identity; it sits ahead-left or centre and is partly hidden whenever the foreground post crosses it. A “cat” mask appears to the right of the post in frames 4–5, matching the nearby animal in RGB, while a small “person” mask at the bottom of frame 5 corresponds only to the camera wearer’s partially visible arm or clothing and is within arm’s reach. The masks clarify that the cat is separate from the stone structure and show both objects’ changing left-right positions as the viewpoint turns, but they contain no direct range information and do not establish facing or gaze. The stone mask changes colour and shape between frames, misses portions, and absorbs or splits nearby surfaces, so object boundaries, occlusion details, and class labels are unreliable.
descriptions.pose: The pose strip is entirely black in all five frames, so it detects no body or hand skeletons and provides no spatial evidence about posture, facing direction, gaze, reach, or motion. It therefore cannot represent the camera wearer’s hands visible near the lower edge of some RGB frames, nor can it describe the cat or the stone structure. Any people beyond the wearer are absent from the RGB context as well, and no person-to-person distances can be established. The empty result is unreliable as evidence that no hands or body parts are present, because the RGB strip contains partial wearer limbs that the pose map failed to detect.
